paragraphs: Roman authority in Britain had collapsed by 410, and over the following decades Angles, Saxons and Jutes from what is now northern Germany and Denmark crossed the North Sea, some as invited mercenaries and others as settlers claiming land. The near-contemporary monk Gildas blamed a leader named Vortigern for inviting them in against Pictish raids, then losing control of the arrangement.

How much was violent conquest and how much was gradual intermarriage is still argued over, since the record shows both mass graves and long stretches of peaceful coexistence. What is not disputed is the outcome: within two centuries lowland Britain's Brittonic-speaking population had largely given way to a patchwork of Anglo-Saxon kingdoms whose language became English and whose borders shaped England's counties.

Every language from Malagasy in the Indian Ocean to Hawaiian and Maori in the Pacific traces back to a single family that began on Taiwan. Around 3000 BCE, Austronesian-speaking farmers began moving south into the Philippines, carrying rice cultivation, distinctive red-slipped pottery, and outrigger canoe technology with them.

What makes the expansion unusual is its scale rather than its speed at any one step. Over the following centuries it fanned out through island Southeast Asia, then out into the remote Pacific and eventually as far as Madagascar off the coast of Africa, making Austronesian the only language family in history to end up spoken on both sides of an ocean it had to be sailed across to reach.

The Bantu expansion began in what is now Cameroon and Nigeria several thousand years earlier, and by around 300 CE its farming and iron-working communities had spread as far as the southern tip of the continent, a migration so gradual it took place over roughly two thousand years rather than any single generation's lifetime.

Linguists can trace the route because the hundreds of Bantu languages spoken today, from Swahili to Zulu, share enough vocabulary and grammar to be reconstructed back to a common ancestor. The migrants brought iron tools and cereal farming into regions previously held by hunter-gatherer and pastoralist peoples, including the ancestors of today's San and Khoekhoe communities, who were pushed into more marginal land as farming populations grew.

The United States and Mexico signed the Mexican Farm Labor Agreement on 4 August 1942, creating a guest worker scheme meant to plug a wartime labour shortage on American farms while American men were drafted. The programme's name came from brazo, the Spanish word for arm, a fair description of what employers were contracting for rather than a whole worker with a family and a life outside the field.

It outlasted the war it was built for by two decades, bringing several million Mexican men north under short-term farm contracts before Congress ended it in 1964 amid complaints about wage suppression and contract abuse. Its recruitment centres, established routes and a labour market accustomed to cheap temporary Mexican workers did not disappear with it, and shaped the undocumented migration that followed.

News of gold in California reached the port of Guangzhou within months of the 1848 discovery, and by 1852 tens of thousands of men from the Pearl River Delta, many escaping the chaos of the Taiping Rebellion, had crossed the Pacific hoping to strike it rich and send money home. American miners called California Gam Saan, Gold Mountain, and most who went intended to return, not to settle.

Many did not strike gold, and built the laundries, restaurants and labour gangs that later dug much of the Central Pacific Railroad through the Sierra Nevada. The communities they founded in San Francisco and smaller mining towns became the first Chinatowns in America, built for mutual support and because a string of discriminatory laws, culminating in the 1882 Chinese Exclusion Act, made clear no wider welcome was coming.

The first wave of Cubans left almost immediately after Fidel Castro took power in January 1959, mostly wealthy and politically connected people who saw the revolution's direction early. Numbers grew fast once Castro nationalised American-owned businesses and aligned with the Soviet Union, and by 1960 tens of thousands a year were arriving in Miami, including over fourteen thousand unaccompanied children sent ahead under Operation Pedro Pan.

The Cuban Missile Crisis briefly halted direct flights in 1962, and Freedom Flights resumed in 1965, carrying hundreds of thousands more over the following years. Miami's Cuban exile community built its own economy and politics around Calle Ocho and Little Havana, reshaping a mid-sized Florida resort town into a majority Latino metropolis within a generation.

Decades of ploughing had stripped the native grasses that once held the southern plains together, and when drought arrived in the mid 1930s the exposed topsoil lifted into storms that buried fences and turned midday skies black as far away as Chicago and New York. Farmers in Oklahoma, Texas, Kansas and neighbouring states, already squeezed by Depression prices, lost entire farms to dust that would not settle.

An estimated three hundred to four hundred thousand people left the region for California, hoping for work in its fields, in a movement Californians lumped together under the label Okies regardless of where migrants had started from. John Steinbeck's The Grapes of Wrath, published in 1939, drew on migrant camps he had reported on, and the exodus pushed the federal government to fund soil conservation programmes.

Steamship fares fell sharply after 1880, cutting an Atlantic crossing from weeks to about ten days and from a fortune to a price a labourer could afford. Emigration from Europe, which had long run mostly from Britain, Ireland and Germany, broadened to include huge numbers from Italy, Poland, and the Russian and Austro-Hungarian empires, many fleeing pogroms and conscription.

Ellis Island opened in 1892 specifically to process the volume, and by the peak years around 1907 over a million immigrants a year were arriving through New York harbour alone. Most came steerage class, in the ship's lowest decks, and the paperwork they filled out there, names sometimes altered by clerks who could not parse an unfamiliar alphabet, still shapes what millions of American surnames look like today.

Over a million people crossed into Europe by sea and by the Balkan land route in 2015, the largest movement of refugees the continent had processed since the Second World War. Most were fleeing the Syrian civil war, but the routes also carried Afghans, Iraqis and Eritreans, funnelled through overloaded dinghies from Turkey to the Greek islands and rickety fences along the Hungarian and Croatian borders.

Germany's chancellor Angela Merkel opened the country's doors with the phrase wir schaffen das, we can manage this, taking in more than a million asylum seekers that year alone, while other EU states argued over quotas and fences went up in Hungary. The photograph of three year old Alan Kurdi, drowned off the Turkish coast in September 2015, briefly shifted European public opinion.

British soldiers began rounding up Acadian farmers in the autumn of 1755, on the order of Nova Scotia's governor Charles Lawrence, who wanted their land cleared and their loyalty to France ended for good. Families were marched onto ships without notice, often separated from each other, and their farms and villages were burned so there was nothing to come back to.

Roughly ten thousand people were scattered across the British colonies, England and France over the following years; conditions on the transport ships killed thousands more. A large number eventually found their way to Spanish Louisiana, where the name Acadian slurred over generations into Cajun, and where their language and cooking survived an ocean and a continent away from the Bay of Fundy.

The American Colonization Society, whose members ranged from abolitionists to slaveholders wanting free Black Americans gone, began sending settlers to West Africa in 1820 and established a permanent colony on Cape Mesurado in 1822. The society's motives were never unified, which is part of why the project drew criticism from Black leaders like Frederick Douglass, who saw it as exile dressed up as opportunity.

The settlers who arrived, many born enslaved with little personal connection to the region, took the name Liberia and in 1847 declared it Africa's first independent republic. The settler minority, called Americo-Liberians, ruled over the indigenous majority for more than a century, a hierarchy whose resentments fed into the coups and civil wars that tore the country apart in the late twentieth century.

West Germany signed a labour recruitment agreement with Turkey in 1961, adding to similar deals already struck with Italy, Spain and Greece, to fill factory jobs during the Wirtschaftswunder boom that its own postwar population could not cover fast enough. The workers were called Gastarbeiter, guest workers, a label that assumed from the start they would eventually go home.

Most did not. Employers found trained workers too useful to let go, families followed the men who had come alone, and by the time recruitment stopped in 1973 several million workers and their children had settled permanently. Germany did not formally recognise itself as a country of immigration until decades later, leaving second and third generation Turkish Germans without straightforward citizenship into the 1990s.

In 376 CE, a large group of Goths asked the Roman emperor Valens for permission to cross the Danube and settle inside imperial territory, fleeing pressure from the Huns further east. Rome had absorbed Germanic groups before, but the numbers this time, and Roman officials' mismanagement of the resettlement, tipped into open revolt within two years, ending in the Roman defeat at Adrianople in 378.

That single crossing is usually taken as the opening act of a period lasting roughly two centuries, as Vandals, Franks and Ostrogoths moved into and carved up the western Roman Empire's territory. Rome's western half did not fall in a single conquest; it was worn down by successive settlements and takeovers by peoples it had spent centuries trying to manage as neighbours rather than subjects.

Edward Hargraves announced a gold discovery near Bathurst, New South Wales in February 1851, having just returned from California convinced the geology looked similar; within months, richer finds at Ballarat and Bendigo in Victoria drew far bigger crowds than his own claim ever produced. Colonial governments, alarmed at losing workers to the goldfields, had actually suppressed earlier gold reports for fear of this disruption.

Migrants poured in from Britain, continental Europe, the United States and China, and Victoria's population roughly tripled during the 1850s as a result. The rapid, largely unregulated growth on the goldfields fed directly into the Eureka Stockade rebellion of 1854, when miners protesting licence fees and a lack of political representation clashed with colonial troops.

Wartime factory labour shortages opened Northern jobs to Black workers in 1916 just as boll weevils were destroying Southern cotton crops, and roughly six million Black Americans left the South for cities like Chicago, Detroit and New York over the following six decades. They were leaving a legal order built to enforce poverty: Jim Crow segregation, sharecropping debts designed never to clear, and the constant threat of lynching.

The Chicago Defender, a Black newspaper smuggled into the South by rail porters, actively promoted the move north and printed train schedules alongside the news. The migration reshaped American cities, seeding the Harlem Renaissance and the sound of Chicago blues, while crowding new arrivals into segregated neighbourhoods that Northern banks and city governments then redlined for decades.

Several thousand Boer families loaded ox wagons and left the Cape Colony from 1836 onward, angered by British rule, the end of slavery without compensation they considered adequate, and land pressure near the coast. They called themselves Voortrekkers, and they moved in scattered parties rather than one column, crossing the Orange and Vaal rivers into country already occupied by Zulu, Ndebele and other African kingdoms.

Fighting followed, most notably the Zulu victory at Italeni in 1838 and the Boer victory months later at Blood River, where a small trekker force held off a much larger Zulu army from behind a wagon laager. The trekkers eventually founded the Boer republics of Natal, the Orange Free State and Transvaal, states whose borders and grievances shaped South African politics for the following century.

Greek colonisation was not driven by a single state but by dozens of independent city-states, each sending out settlers under an appointed founder to establish a new, self-governing polis rather than a dependent outpost. Corinth founded Syracuse in Sicily; settlers from Phocaea founded Massalia, which grew into Marseille; Miletus alone is credited with founding dozens of colonies around the Black Sea.

Population pressure and land shortage at home pushed much of this, alongside opportunities in trade and, in some cases, straightforward exile after political conflict. By around 500 BCE, Greek-speaking cities ringed the Mediterranean and Black Sea from Spain to Ukraine, spreading the alphabet, coinage, and civic institutions that shaped much of the ancient Mediterranean world beyond Greece itself.

Louis XIV's Edict of Fontainebleau, issued in October 1685, revoked the Edict of Nantes that had protected French Protestants for nearly a century, banning their worship outright and forbidding pastors from leaving the country under threat of the galleys. Ordinary Huguenots were technically forbidden to emigrate too, which did not stop them.

Estimates of how many fled range widely, from roughly 150,000 into the hundreds of thousands, smuggled out by fishing boat, on foot over the Alps, and by every route officials could not fully seal. They settled in England, the Dutch Republic, Prussia, and further afield in the Dutch Cape Colony, taking skilled trades such as silk weaving and clockmaking with them and leaving some regions of France measurably poorer for their departure.

Modern humans did not arrive in an empty Europe. Neanderthals had lived there for over 200,000 years, and for several thousand years after around 45,000 years ago the two populations overlapped, sometimes in the same river valleys and cave systems, before Neanderthals disappeared from the record entirely.

Ancient DNA shows the two groups interbred during this overlap: almost everyone outside Africa today carries a small percentage of Neanderthal ancestry, a legacy of unions that left no other trace. Why Neanderthals vanished while the newcomers spread is still debated, with climate swings, competition for game, and sheer population size all argued as causes rather than any single one being settled.

Reaching Australia meant crossing at least sixty kilometres of open ocean, even at the lowest sea levels of the last glacial period, when New Guinea and Australia were joined into the single landmass of Sahul. No boats survive from the crossing, so archaeologists infer it from the only evidence that does: humans on the far side by roughly 50,000 years ago.

That gap of open water is why the crossing gets treated as a milestone rather than a walk. It could not have happened by accident on a raft drifting with the current alone; it implies deliberate voyaging, and possibly repeated attempts, by people with no way to know land lay beyond the horizon. The result was the founding population of Aboriginal Australia, whose continuous cultures are now the oldest living cultures on Earth.

Living through a Siberian winter with Ice Age technology required more than warm clothing. Sites such as Yana in the Russian Arctic, dated to around 30,000 years ago, show people hunting mammoth and woolly rhinoceros and making tools from ivory and bone in a landscape where summer temperatures barely climbed above freezing.

Siberia mattered beyond itself because it was the last staging ground before the Americas. The population that eventually crossed into Alaska is genetically traceable to groups who had spent thousands of years adapting to exactly this environment, making the Arctic less a barrier to the New World than the corridor through which it was reached.

The Japanese archipelago was easier to reach during the last glacial period than it is now, when lower sea levels narrowed the straits from the Korean peninsula and from Sakhalin in the north. People were present by around 38,000 years ago, leaving stone tools and, later, some of the oldest known polished stone axes anywhere in the world.

These earliest arrivals are not the ancestors of most of today's Japanese population in a simple, unbroken line. Later waves of migration from the Korean peninsula during the Yayoi period, roughly two and a half thousand years ago, brought rice farming and mixed with the descendants of these first settlers, whose closest surviving cultural relatives are usually identified with the Ainu of Hokkaido.

New Guinea and the Bismarck Archipelago sit just beyond Sahul, the combined landmass of Ice Age Australia and New Guinea, and reaching them meant another set of open-water crossings on top of the one that had already carried people into Sahul itself. Sites on New Ireland and Manus put people in this stretch of the Pacific by around 40,000 years ago.

This is usually called Near Oceania to distinguish it from the far more recent settlement of Remote Oceania, the islands east of the Solomons that stayed empty for another 37,000 years. The gap between the two shows how much harder the longer crossings were: the short hops between visible islands came first, and it took the invention of more capable canoes to go further.

The Huns appear in the historical record suddenly, moving out of Central Asia and into the lands north of the Black Sea by around 370 CE. Roman and Gothic writers described them mainly through their effect on everyone else, since the Huns left no written accounts of their own and much about their origins and language remains genuinely uncertain.

Their arrival set off a chain reaction rather than a single event. Gothic and other Germanic groups already settled near the Danube found themselves squeezed against the Roman frontier, and it was this pressure, not a Hunnic invasion of Rome itself, that pushed the Goths to cross into imperial territory in 376. Attila's better-known assaults on the empire came only decades later, after the Huns built a far larger confederation.

The ships Whitby and Hesperus left Calcutta in January 1838 carrying around four hundred Indian labourers bound for British Guiana, arranged by the planter John Gladstone to replace enslaved workers freed a few years earlier. The men and women aboard signed contracts, usually five years long, that were sold to them as a route to savings and land but in practice bound them to plantations under conditions close to the system just abolished.

The scheme spread over the following decades to Trinidad, Fiji, Mauritius, Natal and other British colonies, moving well over a million Indians by the time indenture finally ended in 1917. Their descendants now form a substantial share of the population in places like Guyana, Trinidad and Fiji, communities whose Hindi, Tamil and Bhojpuri roots trace back to Bihar and Uttar Pradesh.

Speakers of an early Indo-European language moved into the northwestern Indian subcontinent sometime around 1500 BCE, a migration reconstructed mainly from linguistics and, more recently, ancient DNA, since it left little unambiguous archaeological trace of its own. The language they carried developed into Sanskrit, the language of the Vedas.

For decades the idea of any migration at all was politically contentious in India, read by some as implying that Sanskrit and Vedic culture were foreign imports rather than indigenous developments. Genetic studies over the past decade have found a signal of steppe-related ancestry entering the subcontinent around this period, adding to rather than settling the argument over how large the movement was.

The Magyars had been living as steppe nomads in a region called Etelkoz, north of the Black Sea, when attacks by Bulgaria and then by the Pechenegs forced them to move. Under the leadership associated with Arpad, they crossed the Carpathian mountains into the Carpathian Basin in 895 or 896, settling first along the upper Tisza river.

By around 900 they had pushed further into the sparsely populated Pannonian plain, the territory that became the core of the Hungarian kingdom. For decades afterward Magyar raiding parties ranged as far as Spain and northern Italy, until a defeat at the Battle of Lechfeld in 955 pushed the confederation toward settling permanently and eventually converting to Christianity under King Stephen.

New Zealand was the last substantial landmass on Earth reached by people, settled by Polynesian voyagers around 1300 CE, tens of thousands of years after the first human dispersals out of Africa. Its size and temperate climate, so different from the tropical islands the settlers had left, set the arriving population apart almost immediately.

The moa, giant flightless birds unique to New Zealand, were hunted to extinction within roughly a century of settlement, a speed archaeologists cite as a case study in how fast a founding population without natural predators can reshape an ecosystem. Over the following centuries that population developed the distinct Maori culture and language, adapted to a land far larger and colder than any their ancestors had settled before.

The Chatham Islands lie roughly 800 kilometres east of New Zealand, and estimates for when Polynesian voyagers first reached them vary by centuries, with genealogical and archaeological evidence pointing to settlement somewhere between 1400 and 1500 CE, mostly from New Zealand rather than directly from eastern Polynesia.

Isolated on a small, cool archipelago with limited resources, the settlers developed the distinct Moriori culture, including a tradition, attributed to the ancestor figure Nunuku, that renounced warfare among themselves. That tradition would prove catastrophic centuries later, when Maori invaders arrived from New Zealand in the 1830s and the Moriori chose not to fight back.

Brigham Young led the first wagon company out of Nauvoo, Illinois in 1846 and reached the Salt Lake Valley in July 1847, after the Latter-day Saints had been driven out of Missouri and then Illinois by mobs and, in Missouri's case, an extermination order from the state's own governor. Young reportedly looked over the valley and said this was the right place, a line that has outlived any record of exactly when he said it.

Tens of thousands more followed over the next two decades, some pulling their belongings in handcarts rather than wagons because the church could not supply enough oxen. They built an irrigation system in a near-desert basin controlled by no other government, which was the point: Young had chosen ground far enough from the United States that his church could govern itself.

Farming did not spread through Europe as an idea passed between existing foragers. Ancient DNA shows it arrived with people: farmers from Anatolia moved west along two main routes, one hugging the Mediterranean coast and one following the Danube, carrying wheat, sheep, and settled village life into a continent that had lived by hunting and gathering for tens of thousands of years.

In most regions the newcomers' ancestry came to dominate, though not by simple replacement everywhere. Along parts of the Baltic and in pockets further north, hunter-gatherer populations held on for centuries before farming ancestry caught up, so the spread across Europe took closer to three thousand years to complete than any single migration date can capture.

Around a thousand settlers set out from Missouri in what became known as the Great Migration of 1843, following a route already scouted by fur traders and missionaries but never before travelled by wagon train in such numbers. The journey to the Willamette Valley took five or six months and covered roughly two thousand miles, over the Rockies at South Pass, a gap wide and gentle enough that wagons could cross without unloading.

The trail's early success answered a real question, whether families with wagons and children could cross the continent overland at all, and the answer drew hundreds of thousands more over the following two decades. It also fed an American claim to Oregon Country that Britain had disputed, since American farmers already settled there strengthened Washington's claim more than any treaty could.

No single crossing marks this event. Genetic evidence points to a population, probably numbering in the low thousands, leaving Africa around 70,000 years ago and eventually out-competing or absorbing every other human lineage it met outside the continent, including Neanderthals and Denisovans.

The route is contested: some geneticists favour a crossing of the Bab-el-Mandeb strait into Arabia, others a path up through the Sinai. What is not contested is the consequence. Every population outside Africa, from Scandinavia to Tierra del Fuego, carries the genetic signature of descending from this one dispersal, making it the closest thing humanity has to a shared point of departure.

Some 700,000 Palestinians left or were forced out of their homes between late 1947 and 1949, during the civil war that preceded Israel's founding and the wider war with neighbouring Arab states that followed. Whole towns, including Jaffa, Lydda and Haifa, emptied within weeks under military assault, direct expulsion orders and panic spread by massacres such as the one at Deir Yassin in April 1948.

Palestinians call the exodus the Nakba, the catastrophe, and it remains a live political fact rather than a closed historical one: Israeli law bars the refugees and their descendants, now numbering in the millions, from returning to properties inside Israel. Roughly four hundred Palestinian villages were destroyed or resettled in the process and never rebuilt under their original names.

When British India split into India and Pakistan in August 1947, the border through Punjab and Bengal was drawn by a lawyer, Cyril Radcliffe, who had never visited the subcontinent before and was given about five weeks to finish the map. Roughly fourteen million people crossed it in both directions within months, Muslims moving toward Pakistan and Hindus and Sikhs toward India, in what remains the largest forced migration in recorded history.

Trains arrived at stations already full of dead passengers, and estimates of the killing that accompanied the crossing range from several hundred thousand to two million, a range that has never narrowed because no government kept a full count at the time. Families on both sides still describe partition as the specific week they walked away from a house they never saw again.

Phoenician cities such as Tyre and Sidon, on the coast of modern Lebanon, had little farmland to spare, so their wealth came from trade routes that stretched the length of the Mediterranean and out into the Atlantic. From around 800 BCE they founded trading posts and colonies along those routes, including Gadir, now Cadiz in Spain, and Carthage on the North African coast.

Carthage, traditionally founded around 814 BCE by settlers from Tyre, eventually outgrew its parent city and became the dominant power of the western Mediterranean in its own right, fighting Rome across three Punic Wars centuries later. The Phoenician script the colonists carried with them also underlies the Greek alphabet, and through it, the Latin one still in use today.

The Potsdam Agreement of August 1945 gave the Allies' blessing to something already underway, the removal of ethnic Germans from land handed to Poland and Czechoslovakia at the war's end. Around twelve million people were expelled or fled, most from regions like Silesia, East Prussia and the Sudetenland where German-speaking communities had lived for centuries, sometimes since well before the modern German state existed.

The transfers were meant to be, in the Potsdam text's own words, orderly and humane, but the reality, revenge, winter treks and overcrowded trains, killed several hundred thousand people and by some estimates well over a million. West Germany absorbed most of the survivors, and the political lobby they formed, the expellee associations, remained a force in German politics for decades.

John Winthrop's fleet of eleven ships left England in the spring of 1630, carrying roughly seven hundred colonists to a stretch of coast they had never seen. Winthrop wrote his shipboard sermon on the crossing, imagining the new settlement as a city upon a hill, a phrase later borrowed by presidents who left out the parts about mutual obligation and public failure.

Over the following decade something like twenty thousand more English Puritans followed, fleeing Archbishop Laud's pressure to conform and a king who had stopped calling Parliament. They landed in a colony already governed by a charter its own leaders had smuggled out of England, letting Massachusetts Bay run itself with less royal oversight than any other American settlement of its era.

Rent increases on Ulster estates, a run of poor harvests and restrictions on Presbyterian worship pushed thousands of Scots settled in northern Ireland back onto ships in 1718, bound this time for Boston and the other American ports. Most had been in Ireland for barely two or three generations, planted there under earlier English colonisation schemes, before economic pressure moved them again.

They kept moving once they landed, pushing past the coastal towns that already had established English communities and into the Appalachian backcountry from Pennsylvania down to the Carolinas. That frontier culture, Presbyterian, clannish and famously resistant to outside authority, later supplied a disproportionate share of American backwoods soldiers and, eventually, several presidents.

Egyptian inscriptions name several groups collectively as the Sea Peoples, blamed for attacks on Egypt and, by extension, for the wider collapse that brought down the Hittite Empire, Mycenaean Greece, and cities across the Levant around 1200 BCE. Ramesses III recorded repelling one such attack in his mortuary temple at Medinet Habu, listing peoples whose homelands are still argued over.

Whether these groups caused the Bronze Age collapse or were themselves refugees fleeing it is unresolved. Drought, famine, and the breakdown of long-distance trade in tin and copper were already straining the region's palace economies, and the movement of displaced populations by land and sea looks as much like a symptom of that collapse as its cause.

The Caribbean islands were reached late compared with the American mainland, and not in one wave. The earliest migrants came from Central America and settled Cuba and Hispaniola, moving between islands close enough to see from one shore to the next, a very different kind of voyage from the open-ocean crossings that later settled the Pacific.

Later migrations from the Orinoco basin in South America pushed north through the Lesser Antilles over the following millennia, arriving with pottery and farming that the earlier arrivals lacked. The result was a patchwork of populations layered over centuries, not a single founding people, which is part of why archaeologists still debate exactly when and from where the first islands were settled.

Around 1000 BCE, seafarers of the Lapita culture reached the islands now called Fiji, part of a slow eastward push across the Pacific that had already carried their distinctive dentate-stamped pottery from the Bismarck Archipelago through the Solomons. They travelled in double-hulled canoes without metal tools or instruments beyond the stars, currents and bird flight paths, navigation skills passed down rather than written.

Fiji sat at a crossroads of that migration, close to Melanesia and close to Tonga and Samoa, from where settlers' descendants pushed on into what became Polynesia within a few centuries. Archaeologists trace the whole span of that dispersal, from New Guinea to Hawaii and Easter Island, largely through the broken shards of Lapita pottery left behind at sites like Fiji's.

Hawaii sits roughly 3,700 kilometres from the nearest inhabited islands of eastern Polynesia, a distance that made it one of the last places on the planet settled by humans. Voyagers navigating by the stars, ocean swells, and the flight patterns of birds reached the archipelago by around 1000 CE, without instruments and without knowing land lay ahead.

Experimental voyages on reconstructed double-hulled canoes, most famously the Hokule'a in the 1970s, have since shown the crossing was navigable using only these traditional methods, settling a debate over whether such long-distance Polynesian voyaging was deliberate rather than accidental drift. The settlers carried taro, breadfruit, and pigs, founding one of the most isolated complex societies in the Pacific.

Madagascar lies off the coast of East Africa, yet its earliest language and much of its genetic ancestry trace not to Africa but to Borneo, over six thousand kilometres away across the open Indian Ocean. Austronesian voyagers reached the island by around 500 CE, the far western edge of the same seafaring expansion that had already carried their relatives across the Pacific.

The Malagasy language today is closest to Ma'anyan, spoken by a small community in southern Borneo, a link linguists identified long before genetics confirmed it. Later arrivals from the East African coast and Arabia added further ancestry over the following centuries, but the Austronesian layer, laid down first, remains the clearest trace of how the island was originally reached.

After Austronesian voyagers reached western Polynesia, including Samoa and Tonga, the expansion east into the remote islands of the Society group and the Cook Islands stalled for roughly a thousand years, a gap archaeologists still argue over. By around 1000 CE it resumed, carrying settlers to islands separated by far greater distances of open ocean than anything crossed before.

The voyaging canoes that made this possible were double-hulled and capable of carrying breeding pairs of pigs and chickens along with seed crops, everything a founding population needed to establish itself on land with no prior inhabitants. From these eastern Polynesian islands, further voyages reached Hawaii, Easter Island, and New Zealand, completing the settlement of the Pacific's most remote corners.

Monte Verde, in southern Chile, is the site most often cited for how quickly people spread once they reached the Americas: excavators found the remains of a tent-like structure, wooden stakes, and preserved plant remains far south of the entry point at the Bering land bridge. For decades the site was dated to roughly 14,500 years ago, long before the once-standard Clovis timeline allowed.

That dating is now itself being questioned. Fresh fieldwork published in 2026 has argued the layers are thousands of years younger than the original estimate, reopening a debate that Monte Verde was supposed to have settled. What is not in dispute is that people were living at the southern tip of South America astonishingly soon after the first crossing into Alaska, however the exact arithmetic eventually shakes out.

Slavic-speaking communities are barely visible in written sources before the sixth century, then appear across a huge stretch of Eastern Europe within a few generations. By around 550 CE they were settling former Roman provinces in the Balkans alongside Avar nomads, and spreading north and east across territory that had previously been described, when described at all, in vaguer terms by earlier writers.

Because the sources are so thin, historians still argue over how much of this was mass migration of people versus the spread of a language and identity among populations who were already there. What is clearer is the outcome: within a few centuries Slavic languages were established from the Elbe to the Volga and south into Greece, laying the linguistic map that still divides much of Eastern Europe today.

Soviet Jews had petitioned for years to leave for Israel, and a trickle of exit visas in the 1970s turned into a flood once Mikhail Gorbachev's reforms loosened emigration controls in the late 1980s. As the USSR broke apart in 1990 and 1991, hundreds of thousands left within a couple of years alone, driven by economic collapse, resurgent antisemitism, and finally the freedom to simply apply and go.

Israel's government launched Operation Solomon-style airlifts and direct flights to bring arrivals in quickly, and by the end of the decade over a million former Soviet citizens had settled there, reshaping its politics, its Russian-language press and even its supermarket shelves. A substantial number went to the United States instead, especially to Brooklyn's Brighton Beach, which acquired the nickname Little Odessa.

The Thule people spread rapidly east from Alaska across Arctic Canada around 1200, carrying toggling harpoons, dog sleds and umiak boats that let them hunt bowhead whales far more efficiently than the Dorset culture already there. Within a couple of centuries they reached Greenland, where they met and eventually replaced Dorset communities and, in the south, Norse settlers from Iceland.

How the two groups interacted is still debated, since Norse sagas mention encounters with people they called Skraelingjar but give no coherent account of what followed. What is clear is that the Norse Greenland colonies died out by the fifteenth century while the Thule endured; their descendants are the ancestors of the Inuit populations still living across Arctic Canada and Greenland today.

In 1526, the Spanish explorer Lucas Vazquez de Ayllon sailed from Hispaniola with several ships carrying several hundred settlers and around a hundred enslaved Africans, landing on the coast of what is now South Carolina and founding the short-lived settlement of San Miguel de Gualdape. Within weeks the enslaved men rebelled, burned part of the settlement, and fled into the surrounding country.

That rebellion collapsed the colony and the Spanish survivors withdrew, but the ships that carried it there mark the start of a trade that did not stop. Over the following three and a half centuries, an estimated twelve million or more Africans were forced across the Atlantic in similar holds, a system that long outlasted the single failed settlement that opened it.

The Vandals had already spent two decades on the move, crossing the Rhine into Gaul in 406, then Spain, before their king Geiseric led them across the Strait of Gibraltar into Roman North Africa in 429. Ancient sources put the crossing force at around eighty thousand people, likely counting warriors, families and allied Alans together rather than fighting men alone.

Within a decade Geiseric had taken Carthage, the province's wealthiest city and the source of much of Rome's grain, and built a fleet that raided Sicily and sacked Rome itself in 455. Their kingdom lasted a century before Byzantine forces under Belisarius destroyed it in 534, but the name Vandal outlived the state by well over a millennium, attached ever after to any act of pointless destruction.

After Saigon fell in 1975, an exodus that began among former South Vietnamese officials and the ethnic Chinese business community grew through the late 1970s into a much wider flight, with hundreds of thousands crowding onto small, unseaworthy fishing boats bound for anywhere that would take them. Estimates of how many drowned, were killed by pirates, or vanished at sea run into the tens of thousands.

Refugee camps sprang up across Malaysia, Thailand, Hong Kong and the Philippines to process the arrivals, and the United Nations coordinated resettlement to the United States, Australia, France and Canada for well over a million people by the mid 1990s. Vietnamese communities in cities like Sydney, Orange County and Paris trace directly back to those camps.

The Empire Windrush docked at Tilbury on 22 June 1948 carrying just over a thousand passengers, roughly eight hundred of them from Jamaica and other Caribbean islands, several travelling on a newspaper advertisement offering a cheap passage rather than any formal recruitment scheme. Many had served Britain in the war and came expecting the welcome due to fellow subjects of the same empire.

That welcome mostly did not arrive: landlords and employers turned people away openly, and some arrivals spent their first weeks in a deep air-raid shelter under Clapham Common because no housing had been arranged. The ship's name became shorthand for the whole postwar generation of Caribbean settlement, a history revisited with fresh anger in 2018 when it emerged the Home Office had wrongly deported some of their descendants.

The Yamnaya were pastoralists of the Pontic-Caspian steppe, north of the Black and Caspian seas, who by around 3000 BCE were moving west into Europe in numbers large enough to show up unmistakably in ancient DNA. They are associated with early wagons, horse herding, and burial mounds called kurgans that still dot the steppe from Ukraine to Kazakhstan.

Genetic studies find that the Corded Ware culture, which appeared in central and northern Europe soon afterward, derived roughly three quarters of its ancestry from steppe migrants like the Yamnaya, a scale of turnover that argues against gradual cultural diffusion. Most linguists now tie this migration to the spread of Indo-European languages, ancestral to English, Russian, Hindi and most languages of Europe and South Asia.
